verification.platform: verified on a CRLF Windows checkout, so the section 13 line-ending failures are genuinely fixed
verification.liveSandbox: Verified against real machines in xroga-sandbox, each destroyed after: create, wait for started, exec and force-delete all behave as the provider assumes; base64 file injection lands at the requested guest path; the exec reply field is exit_code; egress denial proven with a control (registry.npmjs.org reachable without the unshare wrapper, denied with it); and an argument containing a shell metacharacter was echoed as literal data with no injected file created. End-to-end after the guest-shape fix: cpus=4 memory_mb=1024 created, ran to exit 0, denied egress, and was destroyed.
verification.leakCheck: xroga-sandbox confirmed to hold no machines, no IP and no secrets after every verification run.
verification.postDeployDefect: The first deploy registered the provider but every create was rejected with HTTP 400 invalid config.guest.cpus, because the default 300 cpuSeconds / 60 gives 5 and Fly accepts only [1 2 4 6 8]. Stub tests could not catch it — they replay this module own arithmetic — so it was found by running the deployed module from the production host. Fixed in PR #466 (allowedCpuCount snaps down; roundedMemoryMb takes the CPU count for the 256-2048 MB per-CPU band). The failure was fail-closed throughout: exitCode null and nothing was executed, never a false pass. Merged as 7dc911b; deploy run 31207648513 succeeded and /health reports that release.
verification.deployedArtefactCheck: Ran /app/dist/sandbox/flyMachineSandbox.js on the xroga-api host at DEFAULT_SANDBOX_LIMITS, which is what compileValidate actually sends because runCmd passes no limits: provider fly-machine available with networkIsolation true; cpuSeconds 300 and memoryMb 2048 computed cpus=4 memory_mb=2048, both legal; execution exited 0 with the injected /work/marker.txt readable; networkPolicy none gave EGRESS_DENIED while networkPolicy registry-only gave EGRESS_ALLOWED through the same code path, so the denial is unshare -n rather than absent connectivity; 0 machines remaining. id -u printed 0, the documented root limitation appearing exactly where the table says it will.

resolvedBlockers.resolution: Closed without the always-on paid worker the original entry assumed was necessary.
resolvedBlockers.why: A Fly app record is free; billing attaches to machines, volumes and IP addresses. So the sandbox app can exist permanently at zero cost and pay only for the seconds a microVM actually runs. The earlier analysis treated an always-on worker as the floor, which overstated the blocker.
resolvedBlockers.approval: Owner approved the ephemeral-machine approach explicitly.
resolvedBlockers.costModel: xroga-sandbox idles with no machines, no volumes and no IP, verified empty. Per execution: one shared-CPU microVM for the duration of the build only.
resolvedBlockers.separateAppIsSecurityNotBookkeeping: Fly secrets are app-scoped and injected into every machine in the app. A sandbox machine inside xroga-api would receive SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY and the GitHub tokens automatically. The provider refuses to run against the API app, so this cannot be misconfigured back into a leak.

honestLimits: Code in a Fly Machine runs as root: unshare -n requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN and the Machines API exposes no per-exec user, so the container providers’ --user 1000:1000 and --cap-drop ALL have no equivalent here.
The guest root filesystem is writable; there is no --read-only plus tmpfs equivalent. Containment is by disposal rather than by permission.

Resource capping is partial: guest.cpus and memory_mb come from the caller limits, but diskMb and maxProcesses are not enforced because the Machines API has no --tmpfs size= or --pids-limit equivalent. A fork bomb or a disk-filling build is bounded by the machine memory and its deadline, not by the stated limit.
All three are why this provider registers behind the container providers rather than in front of them, and why that ordering is pinned by a test.
